title: Discussion & Arguments
description: Debate motions with arguments for and against, counter-arguments, logical fallacies and the phrases you need to discuss like a pro.
intro: In the exam, the examiner will often challenge your opinion. Strong candidates don’t just list arguments – they react to counter-arguments, concede points and still defend their position. Each debate card gives you arguments for both sides and a counter-argument for every point.

exercises.title: Discussion phrase toolkit
exercises.instruction: Sort the phrases by function. These five functions are what examiners listen for in the interactive part of an exam.

items.text: I’m afraid I can’t go along with that.

exercises.explanation: Conceding (admitting the other side has a point) does not weaken your argument – it makes you sound fair and confident. Hedging makes your claims more careful and academic, which is important when evidence is mixed.

exercises.title: Say it carefully: hedging and functions
exercises.instruction: Choose the best answer. Questions 1–3 ask for the most appropriately careful (hedged) statement. Questions 4–6 ask what a phrase is doing.

questions.prompt: Which is the most appropriate way to present this claim in a discussion: “Social media causes depression”?
options: Social media definitely causes depression in all teenagers.
Everybody knows that social media causes depression.
There is some evidence that heavy social media use may be linked to depression in some teenagers.
Social media is basically the same as depression.
questions.explanation: “Some evidence”, “may be linked” and “some teenagers” hedge the claim, which matches the mixed research. The other options overgeneralise.

questions.prompt: Which version of “Influencers lie to their followers” is the fairest?
options: Some influencers do not make it sufficiently clear when content is paid for.
questions.explanation: “Some” and “not sufficiently clear” turn an insult into a precise, defensible criticism.

questions.prompt: Which is the best hedged version of “Phone bans improve grades”?
options: Phone bans tend to be associated with fewer distractions, which could have a positive effect on learning.
Phone bans prove that phones are evil.
questions.explanation: “Tend to be associated with” and “could have” are typical hedging devices.

questions.prompt: What is the speaker doing? “Admittedly, labelling ads is a step in the right direction, but it does not solve the problem.”
questions.explanation: “Admittedly … but …” concedes something to the other side, then states the speaker’s actual position.

questions.prompt: What is the speaker doing? “Could you clarify what you mean by ‘harmful content’?”
questions.explanation: Asking for clarification is a smart strategy in an exam: it shows interaction skills and gives you time to think.

questions.prompt: What is the speaker doing? “So, if I understand you correctly, you’re saying that the problem is the business model, not the technology itself?”
questions.explanation: Paraphrasing what the other person said shows active listening – a key interaction skill.

exercises.title: Match the counter-argument
exercises.instruction: Match each argument with the counter-argument that directly answers it. Then choose one pair and say which side you find more convincing, and why.

pairs.left: Influencers are more authentic than traditional advertising.
pairs.right: Once a creator depends on brand deals, authenticity itself becomes a marketing strategy.

pairs.left: AI labels will protect people from deepfakes.
pairs.right: Labels can be removed, and people with bad intentions will simply not use them.

pairs.left: People who have nothing to hide have nothing to fear from data collection.
pairs.right: Privacy is about control over personal information, not about hiding wrongdoing.

pairs.left: News should be free for everyone, so paywalls are unfair.
pairs.right: Quality journalism costs money; if readers don’t pay, advertisers or other interests will.

pairs.left: Social media gives a voice to people who used to be ignored by the media.
pairs.right: It also amplifies the loudest and most extreme voices, which can drown out others.

pairs.left: Banning anonymous accounts would stop online hate.
pairs.right: Much abuse is posted under real names, and a ban would endanger whistle-blowers and vulnerable users.

exercises.explanation: A good counter-argument attacks the reasoning of the original argument, not the person. In the exam, try the pattern: “That’s a fair point, but it overlooks …”

exercises.title: Spot the fallacy
exercises.instruction: Each statement contains a typical flaw in reasoning (a logical fallacy). Identify it. Knowing these helps you analyse media texts and expose weak arguments in a discussion.

questions.prompt: “If we allow phones during breaks, students will soon use them during lessons, then during exams, and eventually nobody will learn anything.”
questions.explanation: A slippery slope claims that one small step will inevitably lead to extreme consequences, without evidence for each step.

questions.prompt: “Why should we listen to her views on data protection? She has an Instagram account herself.”
questions.explanation: Ad hominem attacks the person instead of the argument. Whether she uses Instagram says nothing about whether her arguments are correct.

questions.prompt: “My opponent wants to regulate social media. Clearly, they want the government to control everything we are allowed to say.”
questions.explanation: A straw man misrepresents the opponent’s position as something more extreme, which is easier to attack.

questions.prompt: “Either we ban smartphones in schools completely, or we accept that our children will become addicted.”
questions.explanation: A false dilemma presents only two options when many others exist (e.g. partial bans, media education).

questions.prompt: “Millions of people use this app every day, so it can’t be harmful.”
questions.explanation: The appeal to popularity (bandwagon fallacy) assumes that something is good or true because many people do it or believe it.

questions.prompt: “My cousin was bullied on that platform, so the whole platform is full of bullies.”
questions.explanation: A hasty generalisation draws a broad conclusion from a single case or very little evidence.

questions.prompt: “Nobody has ever proved that this algorithm is harmful, so it must be safe.”
questions.explanation: An appeal to ignorance treats a lack of evidence as proof. “Not proven harmful” is not the same as “proven safe”.

exercises.title: Debate: social media from 16?
exercises.instruction: Read both sides of the debate. Then complete the tasks below – out loud, with a partner if possible.
exercises.motion: Social media accounts should be banned for everyone under the age of 16.
exercises.context: Several governments have discussed or introduced age limits for social media. Australia, for example, has passed a law setting a minimum age of 16 for accounts on many platforms. Supporters see it as child protection; critics see it as unenforceable and paternalistic.

arguments_for.point: Protecting mental health during a vulnerable phase
arguments_for.explanation: Early adolescence is a period of intense social comparison. Delaying access may reduce pressure from appearance-focused content and online conflicts.
arguments_for.counter: The evidence on cause and effect is disputed, and a ban could cut young people off from support communities, e.g. for LGBTQ+ teenagers.

arguments_for.point: Relieving parents and children of an impossible choice
arguments_for.explanation: If all classmates are on social media, individual families cannot say no without excluding their child. A general rule solves this collective problem.
arguments_for.counter: This could also be solved by better default settings and age-appropriate versions of platforms rather than a total ban.

arguments_for.point: Platforms have failed to regulate themselves
arguments_for.explanation: Most platforms officially require users to be at least 13, yet younger children often sign up anyway. A legal age limit would force companies to take age checks seriously.
arguments_for.counter: Reliable age verification usually requires ID or biometric data, which creates new privacy risks for everyone.

arguments_against.point: Bans are easy to get around
arguments_against.explanation: Teenagers can lie about their age, use VPNs or their parents’ accounts. A ban may simply push them into less visible, less safe corners of the internet.
arguments_against.counter: Laws are not useless just because some people break them; they set norms and put pressure on companies.

arguments_against.point: Young people need to learn to use media responsibly
arguments_against.explanation: Suddenly allowing full access at 16 without any practice could be worse than gradual, guided use with media education.
arguments_against.counter: Learning can start with supervised tools and messaging; full social media with algorithms is not necessary for learning.

arguments_against.explanation: It allows creativity, political participation, friendships and access to information, which a ban would take away.
arguments_against.counter: Many of these benefits are available through other channels, and the risks for younger children may outweigh them.

phrases.label: Taking a position
phrases: I’m against the idea of …, mainly because …
I have mixed feelings about this.

phrases.label: Responding to a counter-argument
phrases: I see where you’re coming from; however, …
That may be true, but it doesn’t change the fact that …

tasks: Choose the side you disagree with and present its two strongest arguments for one minute.
Now present your real position and respond to at least one counter-argument.
Propose a compromise solution that both sides might accept.

exercises.title: Debate: real names only?
exercises.instruction: Study the arguments, then complete the tasks. Try to use at least three phrases from the phrase bank.
exercises.motion: Anonymous accounts should not be allowed on social media.
exercises.context: After cases of online hate, politicians in several countries have called for a “real-name obligation” online. Human rights organisations warn that anonymity protects vulnerable people.

arguments_for.explanation: People may think twice before posting insults or threats if their name is attached.
arguments_for.counter: Many people post hate under their real names, so anonymity is not the only cause.

arguments_for.explanation: Identifying people who commit crimes online, such as threats or fraud, would be faster.
arguments_for.counter: Authorities can already request user data in criminal cases; the problem is often slow procedures, not anonymity.

arguments_for.explanation: Verified identities would make it harder to run networks of fake accounts that manipulate debates.
arguments_for.counter: Verification systems can be faked too, and collecting everyone’s ID creates a huge data-security risk.

arguments_against.explanation: Victims of domestic violence, members of minorities and people exploring their identity may need anonymity to speak safely.
arguments_against.counter: A compromise is possible: platforms could verify identity internally while allowing pseudonyms in public.

arguments_against.explanation: In many countries, criticising those in power under your real name can be dangerous.
arguments_against.counter: Special secure channels for whistle-blowers could exist without allowing anonymity everywhere.

arguments_against.explanation: Anonymity has a long tradition in political writing. People may self-censor if every opinion is linked to their name, employer and family.
arguments_against.counter: Freedom of speech has never meant freedom from responsibility for what you say.

phrases.label: Weighing up
phrases: The risks of … outweigh the benefits of …

phrases.label: Proposing a compromise
phrases: Wouldn’t it make more sense to …?

tasks: Explain the difference between anonymity and pseudonymity, and why it matters in this debate.
Argue for one side for two minutes, including at least one concession.
Decide: which single argument in this debate do you find the strongest overall? Justify your choice.

exercises.title: Debate: who is responsible for posts?
exercises.instruction: This is an extra-challenge debate with legal and ethical complexity. Read carefully, then complete the tasks.
exercises.motion: Social media companies should be legally responsible for all content posted on their platforms, just like newspaper publishers.
exercises.context: Traditionally, newspapers are responsible for what they print, while platforms have been treated more like hosts of other people’s content. In the EU, the Digital Services Act (DSA) requires platforms to act on illegal content once they are notified, and places extra duties on very large platforms – but it does not make them fully liable like publishers.

arguments_for.explanation: Their algorithms decide what millions of people see. By actively amplifying content, they act more like publishers than like neutral hosts.
arguments_for.counter: Choosing an order is not the same as writing or approving content; billions of posts cannot be edited like a newspaper.

arguments_for.explanation: If companies faced liability, they would invest far more in moderation and safer design.
arguments_for.counter: Fear of liability could lead to over-blocking: removing legal content just to be safe, which harms free speech.

arguments_for.explanation: Platforms earn money from advertising like media companies and reach more people than most newspapers, so the same rules should apply.
arguments_for.counter: Different structures need different rules; the DSA’s approach of graded duties may be more realistic.

arguments_against.explanation: Huge numbers of posts and videos are uploaded every minute. Checking everything in advance would be impossible without automated filters that make many mistakes.
arguments_against.counter: Scale is a result of the companies’ own business model; it should not be an excuse.

arguments_against.explanation: Strict liability would push platforms to censor anything controversial, silencing activists, satire and minorities.
arguments_against.counter: Clear legal definitions and appeal procedures could limit over-blocking.

arguments_against.explanation: Only the largest corporations could afford the legal risk and moderation costs, making it harder for new, smaller platforms to compete.
arguments_against.counter: Rules could be graded by size, as the DSA already does for very large platforms.

phrases.label: Precise argumentation
phrases: The underlying assumption here is that …
Taken to its logical conclusion, this would mean …

phrases.label: Concluding
phrases: The most sensible solution seems to be …

tasks: Explain in your own words the difference between a “publisher” and a “host”.
Present the strongest argument for each side in one sentence each.
Give a two-minute statement on whether the EU’s middle way (duties, but not full liability) is the right approach.

exercises.title: Debate: paying for public broadcasting
exercises.instruction: Read the arguments and complete the tasks. Connect the debate to the situation in Austria.
exercises.motion: Every household should pay for public service broadcasting, whether they use it or not.
exercises.context: In Austria, the ORF has been funded since 2024 mainly through a household levy (ORF-Beitrag) instead of the old fee for owning a radio or TV. Similar models exist in other European countries, such as Germany. Supporters say public broadcasting is a public good; critics say people should not have to pay for something they do not use.

arguments_for.point: A public good, like roads or schools
arguments_for.explanation: Independent information benefits everyone in a democracy, even people who never watch the news, because they live in a better-informed society.
arguments_for.counter: Unlike roads, information is available from many private sources today, so the comparison is weak.

arguments_for.explanation: Stable funding allows broadcasters to produce investigative journalism, culture and educational programmes that would not be profitable.
arguments_for.counter: Dependence on politically decided funding can create pressure from governments instead.

arguments_for.point: A shared space in a fragmented media world
arguments_for.explanation: Public broadcasters reach people across different groups and can provide common facts in a polarised landscape.
arguments_for.counter: Many young people hardly use traditional broadcasters, so this shared space is shrinking anyway.

arguments_against.explanation: People should be free to decide which media they pay for, as with streaming services.
arguments_against.counter: Public goods are paid for collectively precisely because individual choice would lead to underfunding.

arguments_against.explanation: A flat fee hits poorer households harder than richer ones.
arguments_against.counter: Exemptions for low-income households can reduce this problem.

arguments_against.explanation: With guaranteed income, they can compete with private media online, which may harm commercial newspapers.
arguments_against.counter: Their online offers can be limited by law to avoid unfair competition.

phrases.label: Comparing systems
phrases: One advantage of this system over … is …

phrases.label: Expressing reservations
phrases: I’m in favour in principle, but …
It depends to a large extent on …

tasks: Explain what a “public good” is and whether you think public broadcasting is one.
Present the case against the motion as convincingly as you can for 90 seconds.
Suggest how public broadcasters could become more relevant for people your age.

exercises.title: Debate: does print have a future?
exercises.instruction: Read the arguments and complete the tasks below.
exercises.context: Print circulation has fallen in many countries as readers move online. At the same time, some publications still sell printed editions, often to older readers or as premium products.

arguments_for.explanation: Most people, especially younger ones, get their news on smartphones.
arguments_for.counter: Some readers, especially older people, still prefer print, and they are a large group.

arguments_for.explanation: Paper, printing and delivery are costly, and news is out of date by the time it is printed.
arguments_for.counter: Print can focus on analysis and background rather than breaking news.

arguments_for.explanation: Producing and transporting paper uses resources.
arguments_for.counter: Digital media also has an environmental footprint through devices and data centres.

arguments_against.explanation: A printed newspaper has no notifications or links, which may encourage deeper reading.
arguments_against.counter: Digital apps can offer reading modes without distractions.

arguments_against.explanation: A printed edition cannot be secretly changed after publication and creates a clear record.
arguments_against.counter: Digital archives with visible correction notes can provide the same transparency.

arguments_against.explanation: Weekly papers and magazines may survive as high-quality products people enjoy paying for.
arguments_against.counter: A niche product is not the same as a future for newspapers as a mass medium.

phrases.label: Predicting the future
phrases: I can’t imagine a world without …

tasks: Give your opinion on the motion in one minute.
Name one thing print does better than digital media and one thing digital media does better.
Describe how you think people will consume news in 2040.

exercises.title: Debate: label everything made by AI?
exercises.instruction: Read the arguments for and against, then complete the tasks.
exercises.motion: All content created with the help of AI should be clearly labelled.
exercises.context: The EU’s AI Act includes transparency obligations for certain AI-generated content, such as deepfakes. But AI is now used in many small ways – for spelling, translation or improving photos – so the question is where to draw the line.

arguments_for.explanation: Audiences have a right to know whether a person or a machine created what they see.
arguments_for.counter: We don’t label other tools, like spell-checkers or photo filters, either.

arguments_for.explanation: Labels make it harder to pass off fake images or voices as real.
arguments_for.counter: People who want to deceive will simply not label their content.

arguments_for.explanation: Artists and writers compete with cheap AI content; labels help people value human work.
arguments_for.counter: A label could unfairly stigmatise creators who use AI responsibly as one tool among many.

arguments_against.explanation: Almost all digital content involves some automated processing. A rule for “all” AI use would be unclear.
arguments_against.counter: The rule could focus on content that is substantially generated or that depicts real people.

arguments_against.explanation: If everything carries a label, people will stop paying attention to them.
arguments_against.counter: Different labels for different levels of AI involvement could keep them meaningful.

arguments_against.explanation: People might assume that unlabelled content is real.
arguments_against.counter: Labels should be combined with media literacy, not replace it.

phrases.label: Defining terms
phrases: It depends on what we mean by …
We need to distinguish between … and …

tasks: Decide where you would draw the line: which kinds of AI use should be labelled, and which should not?
Respond to the counter-argument “People who want to deceive will simply not label their content.”
Sum up the debate in four sentences.

exercises.title: Debate: media literacy as a school subject
exercises.instruction: Read both sides and complete the tasks. Use your own school experience as examples.
exercises.motion: Media literacy should be a compulsory school subject with its own lessons and grades.
exercises.context: Many experts, including UNESCO, call for media and information literacy to be part of education. The question is whether it should be a separate subject or integrated into all subjects. Finland is often mentioned as a country that has made media literacy a priority in schools.

arguments_for.point: It is too important to leave to chance
arguments_for.explanation: If it is everyone’s job, it may end up being no one’s job. A separate subject guarantees time and trained teachers.
arguments_for.counter: A separate subject may isolate the topic, while integrated teaching shows its relevance everywhere.

arguments_for.explanation: Citizens who can recognise manipulation are harder to mislead in elections.
arguments_for.counter: Media literacy alone cannot solve the problem; platform design and regulation matter too.

arguments_for.explanation: Many young people feel unsure how to judge information online and would value practical skills.
arguments_for.counter: Students also complain about a full timetable; another subject means fewer hours elsewhere.

arguments_against.explanation: Checking sources is relevant in history, science and languages, so it should be practised there.
arguments_against.counter: Integration often fails in practice because teachers lack time and training.

arguments_against.explanation: Turning critical thinking into a graded subject could make it feel like just another test.
arguments_against.counter: Project-based assessment can avoid simply testing facts.

arguments_against.explanation: A fixed curriculum may be outdated quickly.
arguments_against.counter: The core skills – questioning sources, checking evidence – stay the same.

tasks: Describe one situation where you learned something important about media at school – or wish you had.
Argue for or against the motion for two minutes.
Design the outline of a short media literacy course for 14-year-olds: three topics you would include.

exercises.title: Debate: online friends, real friends?
exercises.instruction: Read the arguments and complete the tasks below.
exercises.motion: Online friendships are just as valuable as friendships in real life.
exercises.context: Many young people have friends they know only from gaming, forums or social media. Some of these relationships last for years. Others argue that real friendship needs physical presence.

arguments_for.explanation: The internet lets people find others with the same rare interests or experiences, which may not exist in their town.
arguments_for.counter: Shared interests alone don’t make a deep friendship; shared experiences matter too.

arguments_for.explanation: People with disabilities, social anxiety or minority identities may find acceptance online first.
arguments_for.counter: Online friendships can also become a reason to avoid real-life contact.

arguments_for.explanation: Messages and calls can provide genuine comfort, wherever the friend lives.
arguments_for.counter: Physical presence – a hug, practical help – cannot be replaced by a screen.

arguments_against.explanation: Much meaning comes from tone and facial expression, which is lost in text.
arguments_against.counter: Video calls and voice messages restore many of these signals.

arguments_against.explanation: You cannot be sure who someone really is online.
arguments_against.counter: Deception happens offline too, and long-term online friends often meet in person.

arguments_against.explanation: It is easy to disappear online by blocking or ghosting someone.
arguments_against.counter: Commitment depends on the people, not on the medium.

tasks: Share your opinion and give a personal example (real or imagined).
Explain which counter-argument you find most convincing.
Discuss: what makes a friendship “real” in your view?
